:::{#thm-svd}
#### Singular value decomposition

Let $\matr{A}$ be an $n \times p$ matrix with real entries
and $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = r$ (@def-rank).
Then there are
an $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix $\matr{U}$,
a $p \times p$ orthogonal matrix $\matr{V}$ (@def-orthogonal-matrix),
and numbers $\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots \ge \sigma_r > 0$
such that

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{n \times p}
= \underbrace{\matr{U}}_{n \times n}\,
\underbrace{\matr{D}}_{n \times p}\,
\underbrace{\tp{\matr{V}}}_{p \times p}
$$

where $\matr{D}$ has entries $d_{ii} = \sigma_i$ for $i = 1, \ldots, r$
and every other entry $0$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-svd-any-matrix}
#### The SVD applies to every real matrix

The proof is outside the scope of these notes;
see @banerjee2014linear [Chapter 12, Theorem 12.1, p. 373].
Unlike the spectral theorem (@thm-spectral),
@thm-svd applies to every real matrix,
including one that is not square or not symmetric.

For example, the $1 \times 2$ matrix
$\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$
is not square, so @thm-spectral does not apply to it.
It has rank $1$, and @thm-svd holds with
$\matr{U} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix}$,
$\matr{D} = \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix}$,
and $\matr{V}$ the orthogonal matrix $\matr{Q}$ from @exm-spectral,
which is symmetric, so $\tp{\matr{V}} = \matr{V}$:

$$
\ba
\matr{U}\matr{D}\tp{\matr{V}}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(substitute)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiplying by the } 1 \times 1 \text{ identity changes nothing)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(move the scalar to the front)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} \cd 1 + 0 \cd 1 & \sqrt{2} \cd 1 + 0 \cd (-1) \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix multiplication)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} + 0 & \sqrt{2} + 0 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix} \sqrt{2} & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(divide by } \sqrt{2} \text{)}
\ea
$$

$\matr{U}$ is orthogonal because $\tp{\matr{U}}\matr{U} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \end{bmatrix} = \matr{I}_1$,
and the single singular value is $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{2}$.

:::
